q: You find a resident on the floor and you think they may be hurt. What should you do first?
options: Help them back to bed straight away
Stay with them, call for help and press the emergency bell
Go and find a wheelchair
Write the incident report first
why: Stay with the resident, call for help and press the emergency bell. Do not move them if you suspect an injury.
source: POL-001 Falls Prevention and Response, section 4

q: Who decides when a resident who has fallen can be helped up?
options: Any care worker who is trained
The resident
The Registered Nurse (RN) in charge, after assessing
The family
why: The RN assesses the resident before they are moved. Staff may only help them up after the RN says it is safe.
source: POL-001 Falls Prevention and Response, section 4

q: When must the incident report for a fall be completed?
options: Before the end of the shift
Within a week
Only if the resident is hurt
Whenever the RN asks for it
why: Complete the incident report before the end of the shift (see POL-004).
source: POL-001 Falls Prevention and Response, section 5

q: How many trained staff does a full hoist transfer need?
options: It depends on how heavy the resident is
why: A full hoist always needs 2 trained staff.
source: POL-002 Manual Handling and Safe Transfers, section 3

q: You think a resident's ability to move has changed since the care plan was written. What do you do?
options: Use the method you think is best
Use the method from the care plan anyway and say nothing
Stop and tell the RN
Ask a family member
why: Never use a different method from the care plan. Stop and tell the RN.
source: POL-002 Manual Handling and Safe Transfers, section 2

q: Which of these must you never do?
options: Explain to the resident what you are about to do
Check the brakes are on
Pull a resident up by their arms
Use the sling listed in the care plan
why: Never lift a resident manually by yourself, and never pull a resident by their arms.
source: POL-002 Manual Handling and Safe Transfers, section 5

q: When should you clean your hands?
options: Only when they look dirty
Before and after contact with a resident, before handling food, after toileting care and after removing gloves
Only at the start of a shift
Only after using the toilet
why: Clean your hands before and after resident contact, before handling food, after toileting care and after removing gloves.
source: POL-003 Infection Prevention and Control, section 2

q: You have had diarrhoea this morning and you are rostered to work. What should you do?
options: Come to work and wear a mask
Come to work but avoid the kitchen
Do not come in. Tell your manager or the agency before the shift
Come in and tell the RN when you arrive
why: Do not come to work with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever. Tell your manager or the agency before the shift.
source: POL-003 Infection Prevention and Control, section 4

q: Two residents have similar vomiting symptoms. What should you do?
options: Wait and see for a day
Tell the RN in charge immediately
Write it in the notes only
Move both residents to the dining room
why: If 2 or more residents have similar symptoms, tell the RN in charge immediately.
source: POL-003 Infection Prevention and Control, section 5

q: Which of these counts as an incident that needs a report?
options: A near-fall
A resident enjoying lunch
A visitor arriving late
A resident choosing a different TV show
why: Falls, near-falls and injuries count as incidents.

q: What should you write in an incident report?
options: What you think went wrong and who is to blame
Only the facts: what you saw, what time, what action was taken
As little as possible
Your opinion about the resident
why: Write only the facts. Do not guess or blame.

q: You are an agency worker and your shift is ending after an incident. What must you do?
options: Complete the incident report and hand over verbally to the RN before leaving
Leave it for the next shift
Send the agency a message
Tell the resident's family
why: Agency staff must also complete the incident report and hand over verbally to the RN before leaving.

q: What should you check before serving a meal or drink?
options: The weather
The resident's name, texture level and allergies on the care plan or dining list
Only the allergies
Nothing if you served them yesterday
why: Check the resident's name, texture level and allergies on the care plan or dining list.
source: POL-005 Texture-Modified Diets, Thickened Fluids and Choking, section 3

q: How long should a resident stay sitting upright after a meal?
options: 5 minutes
10 minutes
30 minutes
No need
why: Sit the resident upright, at 90 degrees, for meals and for 30 minutes afterwards.
source: POL-005 Texture-Modified Diets, Thickened Fluids and Choking, section 3

q: A resident is choking but can still cough. What should you do?
options: Give them water
Encourage them to keep coughing and press the emergency bell
Slap them hard on the back at once
Leave to find the RN
why: Call for help, press the emergency bell and, if they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
source: POL-005 Texture-Modified Diets, Thickened Fluids and Choking, section 5

q: Which of these must you tell the RN straight away?
options: A resident is eating or drinking much less than normal
A resident likes their new cardigan
A resident asked for the radio to be turned up
A resident went for a walk
why: Eating or drinking much less than normal is a change to report straight away.
source: POL-006 Reporting Changes in a Resident's Condition, section 3

q: What is the role of care staff when a resident's condition changes?
options: Diagnose the problem
Notice and report. The RN assesses and decides
Change the care plan
Wait until the next shift
why: Care staff do not diagnose. They notice and report. The RN assesses and decides what happens next.
source: POL-006 Reporting Changes in a Resident's Condition, section 2

q: After you tell the RN about a change, what else must you do before the end of your shift?
options: Nothing
Write it in the progress notes
Phone the family
Move the resident to another room
why: Tell the RN what you saw, when and what is different from normal, then write it in the progress notes before the end of your shift.
source: POL-006 Reporting Changes in a Resident's Condition, section 4
